changes.before: A short declaration introduces a local variable.
changes.after: Give a value a name so you can use it later.

before: Before this: Go lesson 1, Display text. You will reuse the earlier display function and value names.
A variable is a name that refers to a stored value. Here the value is text, called a string.
Inside a function, topic := "Stars" declares topic and assigns its initial value. Go infers the type from that value.
fmt.Println(topic) reads the variable. With quotes, "topic" would mean literal text instead.

Complete example to read, not an in-app run:
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    topic := "Stars"
    fmt.Println(topic)
}
```

Expected output from this example, explained rather than executed here:
```text
Stars
```
after: You already used `fmt.Println` to show text. Now give the text a name first.
A variable is a named place for a value. Text is a kind of value called a string.
Inside a function, `topic := "Stars"` creates the variable topic and stores Stars in it. `:=` lets Go work out the kind of value from what you give it.
`fmt.Println(topic)` reads the value stored in topic. With quotation marks, `"topic"` means the word topic itself.

Follow the value from its name to the screen.
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
    topic := "Stars"
    fmt.Println(topic)
}
```
The screen shows `Stars`, the value stored in topic.
